prize_parts.citation: For developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets from market data.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged from round 1: B005 with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The chair asks for one test applied to all candidates. Mine is: did the work change what can be credibly known, has that been validated over time in use or in independent evidence, and can the credit be assigned without contested exclusions? B005 meets all three. Random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices made substitution patterns, market power and welfare measurable from market data, in the way new historical series made long-run growth measurable. Merger review, trade, health and environmental analysis use it routinely, and about three decades of replication and critique are available, so the Committee can judge durability from evidence. The three authors of the estimator form a coherent credit set. Friberg's move from Bresnahan to Levinsohn removes the main attribution split among supporters. The same test treats the others as follows. B030 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) has strong design-based evidence and a clean trio, but magnitude and persistence are still debated. B027 has very high conceptual originality and the cleanest credit, but its validation is indirect. B014 is mature and coherent, but its cross-country identification is weaker. B005 comes out ahead on this test, and I accept that this is a judgement. Five members naming B005 is not evidence of merit and I do not use it as such. My position changed in one respect. I now treat B030, not B036, as an alternative. Colleagues convinced me that B036's credit cannot be cut to three names without contested omissions, whereas the B030 trio is the one I proposed in my opening. B005 stays above it because the evidence there has had longer to stabilise.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B005 is a toolkit without a single headline finding. If the Committee holds that a prize should reward a finding about the economy over a way of finding it, B030 or B025 is stronger on that dimension. The credit set is also contestable. Bresnahan and Reiss founded the earlier empirical-IO tradition, and Benkard and Levin made dynamic-model contributions, so any three-name cut excludes people with real claims. A citation that rests on the demand-estimation core answers this only by narrowing the prize. Structural estimates also depend on functional form, instruments and equilibrium assumptions, so applied credibility varies. I have not verified the identification debates beyond what colleagues state.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B014. He argues that Persson, Tabellini and Besley explain policy choice under given electoral and constitutional rules, which differs from the 2024 prize on the long-run origins of institutions. He concedes that cross-country identification is weaker than in design-based work and says he would move to B005 if the overlap were judged decisive.
responses.response: The distinction is fair for the Persson-Tabellini core, and I rate B014 as stronger than my opening rank of seventh implied. As an economic historian, I still think Besley's state-capacity and accountability strand sits closer to the historical-institutions agenda recognised in 2024. That makes Besley the name most exposed to the overlap objection. If B014 is pursued, a Persson-Tabellini core, as Fredriksson offers as a fallback, would be cleaner than the trio. My main remaining difference with the chair is identification. The programme's influence runs through theory plus evidence, but that is a weaker basis for a causal claim in a citation than a method validated by repeated use. I also appreciate his offer to move to B005 and do not treat it as a concession I need.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B027 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the 2022 prize concerned bank runs, intermediation and the Great Depression, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral-constrained borrowers and the feedback between asset prices and credit. He accepts that empirical validation of the mechanism is indirect and would not add Gertler or Gilchrist.
responses.response: That answer weakens the 2022-overlap objection I raised when I ranked B027 eighth. The mechanisms are different, and I now regard the overlap as a weight to consider, not a bar. I agree with leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist, because the accelerator strand is tied to Bernanke. What remains between us is the test. I give more weight to validation in use, and he acknowledges that this is B027's weak point. I would not call B027 weak. The two-alternative limit, not a judgement that it is out of contention, is why it is not among my alternatives. If colleagues weight conceptual originality over documented use, B027 is the case where that choice would be most defensible.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B030 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She treats the China-shock design as a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution, leans toward Dorn over Katz because Katz's skill-bias strand sits close to the 2023 prize, and accepts that persistence, magnitude and shift-share identification are still debated.
responses.response: Her answer changes my view of B030. She would anchor the citation in the empirical labour-demand effects of technology and trade shocks, and not claim the whole task framework. That addresses my earlier worry that credit extends to people outside the ballot, such as Acemoglu. She also persuades me that adjacency to a recent prize does not itself count against a contribution. I propose the same trio. I still put B005 first because the maturity and robustness record is longer. The persistence debate she acknowledges is real, and a claim about persistent local effects is harder to state in a citation than a method validated across thousands of applications. B030 is now my first alternative. If the Committee judges the technology and trade strands to be separate achievements, I would favour the China-shock work alone, as she suggests.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first and, after reading the openings, moved his third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn. He says a demand-estimation citation should credit all three authors of the paper it rests on. He keeps B025 and B030 as alternatives and notes that B025 depends on weighing Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
responses.response: His revision resolves what I saw as the main attribution disagreement among supporters, and I am glad to be on the same names. I also take his point that field proximity can bias a member's view. I am not an IO specialist, and my case for B005 is a measurement argument from economic history, which is why I want the citation tied to the estimator and not to the wider tradition. I share his view on B025. The Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum question is what moved me from B025 in round 1, and nothing in round 1 resolves it. B025 remains an alternative because the foundational economics is strong, but I would not make it a preferred part without a clear answer on that credit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee will frame an IO prize around the demand-estimation core or the broader empirical-IO tradition, which would bring Bresnahan or Reiss back in and require a different citation.
Whether a measurement contribution is held to meet the bar against more substantive findings (B030, B025). Members do not share a common test, and mine is one defensible choice.
How far the persistence and magnitude debate on China-shock effects should lower B030's maturity. I cannot resolve it from the evidence supplied.
Whether Besley belongs with a Persson-Tabellini core, and whether the 2024 overlap affects B014. My view on the historical-institutions link rests on general knowledge, not on verified evidence.
Claims about replication, citation counts and prior prizes come from members' own statements and I have not verified them independently.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for any credited name on B005, B030 or B025. My profile shows institutional proximity to Tommy Andersson, a Lund colleague who also prefers B005, and to Jan Teorell, formerly at Lund, so agreement with Andersson should not be read as independent confirmation. I note the unreconciled discrepancy about Teorell's possible link to Persson that the chair flags. I cannot settle it from my profile and do not adjudicate it. My field is economic history and is not adjacent to industrial organisation, but my reasoning relies on an analogy with historical measurement, which a reader may weigh as a bias. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
